item.content:encoded:
I like it. Simple and to a point.

On it's response to cheating, I had a thought. How do you think it would react to someone who doesn't know they are cheating or otherwise making an illegal move? I had an amusing thought of a D class being tossed to the board, saying "I…I've never played before…" to be told by researchers "Cool story bro, sit down and play or be terminated". D class makes an illegal move, only to have his hand stopped in mid move by an unseen force. He then puts the piece down and then, with casual glances at something unseen on the other side of the board, selects a different piece. 20 moves later, D class wins, noting "Wow, that guy's pretty nice". D class noted to now have a working knowledge of the game.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
It's not BAD, per se. However, there's nothing that grabs me and makes it memorable, either. It's bland, and that's a bad thing, but the article itself isn't poorly written, doesn't contain stupid ideas, and basically it has all the hallmarks of something that should be savable.

The best way to save this is, I feel, to add some depth to why this chess set always wins. Maybe it's able to learn from its opponents, so it wasn't originally impossible to defeat, but now it is; having played the best chess players in the Foundation, it can now beat them all, and by the time computer programs that 'should' have been able to beat it were developed, 177 had already played enough weaker computers to know how to beat them.

Maybe it actually has its own style, modeled after someone like Petrosian, but with a phenomenal aptitude for pure positional play—the kind of play that lends itself toward beating the top computer programs. Humans find themselves unable to make headway against its defensive play, and eventually miss a complication that 177 has created and it exploits the weakness.
